newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Debate rages over NATO enlargement.
newsitem.headline: Debate rages over NATO enlargement.

text.p: NATO's expansion to include at least some former Warsaw Pact countries of central and eastern Europe is now the number one foreign policy objective of U.S. President Bill Clinton's second term.
But, since Clinton's reelection last November, the plan has come under increasing attack from critics both at home and abroad who say it is costly, unnecessary and even dangerous.

Supporters say the the plan is a moral and political obligation which will spread stability by underpinning the new democracies and securing a new role for NATO, the West's military alliance that won the Cold War.
Some even argue that, had enlargement swiftly followed the collapse of communism, the wars which accompanied the break up of former Yugoslavia might have been prevented.

Opponents from Mikhail Gorbachev, the last leader of the Soviet Union, to George Kennan, one of the U.S.'s main arms control specialists and a former ambassador to Moscow, say it will antagonise Moscow and create a new dividing line in Europe.
Kennan wrote in an article in the New York Times that it would be "the most fateful error of American policy in the entire post-Cold War era."

Moscow has fiercely fought the proposal, but recently indicated it could live with a limited enlargement including perhaps Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland, but under no conditions former Soviet republics such as the Baltic states.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana has told Reuters that the new democracies of eastern Europe, doomed to 50 years of communism after World War Two, had a right to join the Euro-Atlantic club.

He and others argue that enlargement will fill what otherwise could become a dangerous security vacuum and hold out an example of what types of benefit await other countries emerging from dictatorship.
Two of NATO's main conditions for membership are democratic control of the armed forces and a market economy.

Sceptics say several countries may meet membership terms but not qualify for political reasons -- at least not in the first, and possibly, only wave. They also say that now is not the time to spend money upgrading their military forces.
They point out that the countries most in need of membership both as an assurance against resurgent nationalism in Russia and as a catalyst for stability are those least likely to get in.
"There is a tremendous amount of double-talk," said one independent analyst.
NATO has made it clear that its expansion into eastern Europe will go ahead whatever happens and a special summit in Madrid in July will invite the first new members to join.
At the same time, alliance leaders say they want expansion to go hand-in-hand with a new post-Cold War relationship with Russia.
The critics say the countries which wish to join face no security threat at present and will face even less of one as, if expected, the deal with Russia is clinched.
They argue that NATO already has difficulty reaching a consensus with its current 16 members and will become unwieldy with any more.
Those in favour argue that the alliance, the only organisation tying North America to Europe, must adapt if it is to survive the end of the Cold War -- the reason for its creation.
